analysis.one_liner: Imposes fines and personal liability on for-profit colleges that mislead students or game loan default rates.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by eight Senate Democrats, was referred to the Senate's education committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill cracks down on for-profit colleges in three main ways: it stops schools from gaming the federal loan default rate that decides whether they keep federal aid, it lets the Education Department fine schools up to millions of dollars for misleading students, and it makes executives personally liable for the costs when their school breaks the rules. Money collected in fines goes into a fund that pays relief directly to students harmed by a sanctioned school. State attorneys general would also get a new power to sue these schools in court.
analysis.who_benefits: Students at for-profit colleges who are misled about job placement, costs, or transferable credits. They gain real financial relief funded by fines on their schools, plus tighter rules that stop schools from hiding poor outcomes by shuffling campuses or pushing borrowers into temporary payment holds.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Education Department to recalculate a school's loan default rate using corrected data whenever the school engaged in 'default manipulation' — tricks like splitting into branches, changing ownership, or putting borrowers in repeated temporary payment holds to hide how many students default.

Creates civil penalties of at least $100,000 — and up to $3 million times a school's default risk for repeat violations — for schools that substantially misrepresent their programs, costs, graduation outcomes, or employability of graduates.
Directs 100 percent of collected penalties into a Student Relief Fund that pays financial relief to students enrolled at schools that break the rules or get sanctioned.

Lets the Education Department hold executives of for-profit schools personally liable for financial losses tied to enforcement actions, and lets the government pursue executives and board members directly to recover federal loans discharged due to school misconduct.
Bars any individual found guilty of defrauding students from serving on the board or as an executive of a for-profit school, as a condition of keeping access to federal student aid.
Gives state attorneys general a new cause of action in court to enforce the misrepresentation rules and win refunds, restitution, and damages for students.

analysis.who_pays: Owners, executives, and board members of for-profit colleges, who face fines sized to their schools' default rates, personal liability for enforcement-related losses, and bans on executives who defrauded students.

drawbacks.text: The default-manipulation definition covers common business acts — adding branch campuses, changing ownership or control, and repeated forbearance — so legitimate restructuring could be penalized, and the Secretary gets wide discretion to decide what counts as 'any similar device or practice.'

Heavy penalties and personal liability could push marginal schools out of the federal aid program or out of business entirely, leaving enrolled students scrambling to transfer — the same shutdown disruption the bill is trying to protect students from.

The Student Relief Fund is financed only by penalty collections (with an authorization for appropriations through 2023), so relief for harmed students depends on how much is actually collected and how well enforcement works in practice.
Because violations accrue across all affiliated campuses and identification codes under common ownership, a problem at one branch could trigger penalties across an entire school system.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is well-targeted at a documented pattern — for-profit schools misrepresenting outcomes and gaming default-rate sanctions — and it includes due process protections: penalties require notice and a hearing, emergency actions are time-limited, and suspension is capped at 60 days unless termination proceedings begin. The honest trade-off is that the strongest medicine, cutting a bad school off from federal aid, also strands its current students, and the relief fund is only as large as the fines collected. On balance the protections outweigh the disruption risk, but enforcement quality would decide the result.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Christopher Murphy introduced the Students Before Profits Act on September 11, 2017, joined by six Democratic cosponsors: Sens. Blumenthal, Brown, Durbin, Franken, Harris, and Warren.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote occurred before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners, executives, and boards of for-profit colleges are better off because the bill never advanced — they avoid fines sized to their default rates, personal liability for enforcement losses, repayment claims for discharged loans, and a ban on hiring executives convicted of defrauding students.

for.name: Sen. Christopher Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Students Before Profits Act of 2017 in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Blumenthal, Brown, Durbin, Franken, Harris, and Warren
for.role: Six Democratic cosponsors in the Senate
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill on the day it was introduced.

against.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee to which the bill was referred and never scheduled it for a hearing or markup during the remainder of the 115th Congress.

against.name: For-profit college industry
against.role: Colleges and operators targeted by the bill's penalties and liability provisions
against.what_they_did: The sector has long opposed tougher federal oversight of its access to student aid, including the risk-sharing and gainful-employment rules of this era.

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors and cosponsors were Senate Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-chaired committee never took the bill up.

industries.note: The bill's entire enforcement apparatus — default-rate recalculation, fines up to $3 million times default risk, executive personal liability, board bans for fraud, and state AG lawsuits — aims at this sector's business model of enrolling students using federal aid while misleading them about cost and outcomes. Its interest in keeping federal aid dollars flowing without these conditions runs directly against students and taxpayers.

By recovering discharged loan costs from executives and boards and tightening eligibility, the bill shifts losses from federal loan programs and taxpayers back onto the schools whose conduct caused them.
